prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B024, Katori and Ye, as a single part. After round 1 the case rests on three things I can check as an experimentalist. First, the idea is distinct: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trap-induced light shift while keeping thousands of neutral atoms, and that is what raises the statistical power by orders of magnitude. It is not a refinement of the comb or of ion control. Second, the number is believed: accuracy and stability near 1e-18 have been reproduced in Sr, Yb and Hg at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and inter-laboratory comparisons and centimetre-scale height measurements are routine. Third, the credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, since every file that discusses B024 names the same two people. The citation should name the lattice clock and its realization at 1e-18, and should not mention the redefinition of the second, which has not happened. I would also keep the invention and realization wording, and leave the many-body physics inside the clock to the supporting text, since Ye's group's work on interactions strengthens the physics case but should not widen the credited achievement.
statement.case_against: The honest objections are still novelty and boundary. Precision frequency metrology was honoured in 2005 (comb) and 2012 (ion control), and a sceptic can read a lattice clock as the next step in that lineage. The two-name credit passes over Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups, and some will see the line between Katori's concept and Ye's record accuracy as engineering and systematics control. Five of eight prefer it, but three of us ranked it sixth or seventh at opening, and support counts are not a substitute for the science. Finally, B003 offers a new regime of matter and a prediction followed by a discovery, which is a more striking pattern than a quantitative leap in an existing capability, and I should not dismiss that.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B003 first, as a specific prediction (the magic twist angle) answered by nature, and sees B024 as a quantitative leap in an existing field, while saying he would be content to see B024 first.
responses.response: I take the prediction-then-discovery pattern seriously and B003 is my first alternative. But I do not think a lattice clock is only a quantitative leap. Without the magic-wavelength condition the trapped-atom light shift limits the accuracy, so the idea is what makes the new regime reachable at all, and the results are reproduced by five groups. For B003 the question is not whether the flat bands were predicted correctly, which they were, but whether the credit and the physics are settled. The pairing mechanism is still debated, twist-angle disorder limits sample reproducibility, and Cao and other early experimenters are outside any three-name credit. Your willingness to see B024 first is what I will rely on, and I would not oppose B003 in a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B003 and argues that the field is only a few years short of consolidation, while he calls B024 a clear and very important invention and would not oppose it as a strong second choice.
responses.response: I accept your own reservation, that the origin of the superconductivity and the correlated phases is still debated, as the main reason I would wait a year or two on B003 and not as a mark against its quality. The Nobel Prize has not required a settled mechanism, so I will not hold that line rigidly. What persuades me to put B024 first is the credit: the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero experiments need Cao in the story, whereas B024 needs nobody outside the two names for the invention and the record. If the committee prefers B003 I would want the citation to name the discovery of correlated states and not imply complete experimental credit, and I would keep Bistritzer as first author of the prediction.

responses.point: Kroll supports B024 and wants the many-body and interaction physics in the clock considered, while noting that Ye's role is partly engineering and systematic control and that the Hall lineage is a possible conflict.
responses.response: I would not put many-body physics in the citation. It is real and Ye's group did it first, but the prize rests more securely on the invention and the 1e-18 realization, and widening the text invites the question of who else did many-body clock work. On Ye's contribution, I do count systematics control at this level as part of the realization: a result that no one else could reproduce would not be a prize result, and five groups have. On your lineage with Hall, thank you for declaring it. I do not think it requires recusal, since you have no collaboration with the credited names, but the committee should record it.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B024, says the redefinition of the second must not be a condition, and judges B014 her main alternative, noting that Takamoto and Katori's 2005 demonstration was the first lattice clock while SYRTE and NIST contributions would take us past two names.
responses.response: I agree that the historical boundary is Katori's proposal and first Sr lattice clock, with Ye's group carrying it to the record accuracy, and that naming SYRTE and NIST would push beyond two names. You are better placed than I am to say whether Takamoto's role in the 2005 demonstration should be in the citation, and I take your answer to be that the invention is Katori's. I would leave Takamoto, Lemonde and Ludlow in the supporting text. I accept your point that the pending redefinition should not be a condition, and I will not write it into the citation. I also agree with you that B014 is a later-year candidate and not a partner for B024 now.

responses.point: Johansson, who first ranked B043, now prefers B024 and asks that the first demonstrations be checked; he lists B023 and B014 as alternatives.
responses.response: Thank you for moving to B024 and for saying openly that your B043 ranking should be discounted. I agree the first demonstrations should be checked, and the record supports the boundary: Katori's 2003 proposal, the 2005 Sr realization with Takamoto, and the JILA 1e-18 results. I do not see a claim that is stronger than Katori and Ye for the invention and the sustained record. On B043 I do not see a reason to change my view that the 2025 circuit prize makes it premature, and the omission of Wallraff makes the credit weaker.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B006 alone, a minimal model with universal hydrodynamic and renormalization-group consequences, and states the reservations himself: partial tests of the Toner-Tu exponents, a loosely bounded field and the omission of Tu.
responses.response: The Toner-Tu argument that order survives in two dimensions out of equilibrium is elegant, and I can follow it. As an experimentalist, my test is whether the quantitative exponents have been measured independently, and by your own statement they are only partially tested. I cannot judge from my field which experiments count, and I would want the condensed-matter members to say so. Tu's omission is also a real weakness for a three-name credit. On B024, you said you would not seriously oppose colleagues, which I take as acceptance, and it was not my aim to bring you to it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct invention and not a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 lineage; Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig give that overlap weight.
Whether the first demonstrations (Takamoto and Katori, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley) change the two-name boundary; I rely on Lindroth and Kroll, who know the atomic physics better than I do.
Whether a prize that does not wait for the redefinition of the second will look early to outside readers; I think the physics does not need it.
Whether B003 should be preferred in a later year, and whether Bistritzer must be in the credit then.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B024: I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye. I am an astroparticle experimentalist, close in subject to B035 and B010 through PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur, but not with the credited names, and I would flag proximity if B035 were taken up. As chair I note Kroll's lineage link to Hall and Lindroth's and Olsson's field proximity, which the committee should record and which do not in my view require recusal on B024.
